not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.

L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference

to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.

oral-bioavailability outcome.

records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is a glipizide-like sulfonylurea sharing the N-cyclohexylsulfonylurea core with glyburide; L4 Caco-2 data for glyburide show high absorptive permeability (Papp 18.1 ± 0.8 ×10^-6 cm/s; 24.9 ± 5.7 ×10^-6 cm/s with Pgp inhibition), supporting efficient intestinal absorption for this chemotype despite ionization.

Glyburide solubility in fasted human intestinal fluid is 5–66 µg/mL (thermodynamic HIF solubility 9.2–15.4 µg/mL), and glyburide formulations show complete release in FaSSIF, indicating that luminal dissolution is not an inherent barrier to absorption for this sulfonylurea class.

Low aqueous solubility values for related sulfonylureas (glibenclamide intrinsic 350 ng/mL; glimepiride 1.6–8 µg/mL in water/buffer) are raw-material/medium-specific and are outweighed by the high permeability and intestinal-fluid solubility; they do not affirm F<20%.

L3 oral-exposure records for glyburide, glimepiride, gliclazide, and tolbutamide show substantial systemic AUC/Cmax after oral dosing in humans (e.g., glyburide AUCss 525.7 ng·h/mL; glimepiride AUC0-∞ 1215 ng·h/mL; gliclazide AUC0-∞ 56.32 µg·h/mL), consistent with F≥20% for the sulfonylurea class.
All visible L1 direct F records are ≥20% (esaxerenone 90.8%, benazeprilat 27.1–28.5%, praziquantel 27.2%), so no direct gold record supports F<20%.

L5 gut-wall efflux/intestinal metabolism evidence has not yet been assessed; glyburide shows some Pgp sensitivity (C125), and its impact on glipizide is unknown.
